passage: Class teacher's note, Class 7. Some parents told me about the children's class chat group. Yesterday someone posted a photo of Pema asleep on the bus with a laughing caption. Damini, who is the group admin, deleted it within minutes and wrote, "We don't post people without asking. Would you want that?" Then she messaged Pema privately to say it was gone. Today she asked me if she could make three group rules. I have said yes, and I will give ten minutes of class time on Monday for everyone to agree on them together.

qa.q: What did Damini write after deleting the photo?
qa.a: "We don't post people without asking. Would you want that?"

qa.q: Why did Damini message Pema privately?
qa.a: She seemed caring and concerned about how Pema felt, and wanted Pema to know it had been dealt with. 🤍

qa.q: Why is letting the class agree the rules together a good plan?
qa.a: Rules everyone helps make are more likely to be respected than ones handed down.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when she learned about the photo?
qa.a: Embarrassed at first, but relieved that someone stood up for her and removed it quickly.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a girl taking ownership of respectful behaviour in a class chat group.

passage:
Diary, Tuesday.
New rule for me (my own): homework before Uday and I watch anything. I did maths first today, even the long division, and nobody had to remind me. Then I fed the building cat that sleeps near the lift. Some people shoo her, but I've taken charge of her water bowl. I found a chips packet thrown on the stairs and put it in the dustbin, even though I didn't throw it. Uday said, "Why do you care, Ira? It's not ours." I said, "The stairs are everybody's, so they're ours too."

qa.q: Where does the building cat sleep?
qa.a: Near the lift.

qa.q: Why did Ira pick up a packet someone else threw?
qa.a: Ira feels the shared stairs belong to everyone, Ira included, and so wants to take care of them.

qa.q: How could Ira get Uday to share this view?
qa.a: Invite Uday to help with the cat's water bowl, so Uday feels a small ownership of the building too.

qa.q: How does Uday see the stairs differently?
qa.a: To Uday they're not their responsibility, since neither of them made the mess.

grounding: It shows a child owning their homework, caring for a building cat and looking after a shared space.

passage: After the village fair, the ground around the pond was littered with paper plates and plastic cups. Most people walked past. Mridul, eleven, and his friend Manoj brought two gunny sacks and started picking. An old man watching said, "The panchayat will clean it." Mridul said, "We swim here. The buffaloes drink here." They worked till the sun went down, pulling cups out of the reeds. Manoj found a duckling tangled in a plastic ring and carefully cut it free with his pocket scissors. The next Sunday, three more children came with sacks.

qa.q: What did the boys use to collect the litter?
qa.a: Two gunny sacks.

qa.q: What does "We swim here. The buffaloes drink here." show about Mridul's thinking?
qa.a: He feels responsible for the pond and protective of it, seeing it as his own and his village's rather than leaving it to the panchayat.

qa.q: How could the village build on what the boys started?
qa.a: Put bins out at the next fair and let children lead a regular clean-up with adult help.

qa.q: What might the old man have felt watching them work until sunset?
qa.a: He may have been surprised and a little moved, since he expected the panchayat to do it.

grounding: It shows village boys taking ownership of a shared pond and caring for its animals.

passage: Every Saturday in their block in Kraków, the courtyard bins overflowed, and the neighbours blamed each other. Jana, nine, noticed pizza boxes stuffed whole into the paper bin, blocking it. Some were her family's. She fetched scissors, flattened them, and showed her little sister Dalia how the pieces slid in easily. 'That's not our job,' Dalia said. 'Half of it is,' said Jana. Then she wrote a sign in careful letters, PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!, and taped it to the lid with a small drawing of a smiling box. By the next Saturday, Mr. Nowak from the ground floor was flattening his too, and he waved at Jana from his window.

qa.q: What did Jana write on the sign?
qa.a: PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!

qa.q: What did Jana mean by 'Half of it is', and what does it show about her?
qa.a: She seemed a little guilty that some of the mess was her own family's, so she felt it was fair to fix it rather than blame the neighbours.

qa.q: Why did the sign work better than complaining would have?
qa.a: It was friendly, clear and showed an easy fix, so neighbours could copy her without feeling accused.

qa.q: How might Mr. Nowak have seen Jana after the sign went up?
qa.a: His wave suggests he appreciated her effort and felt friendlier towards her.

grounding: Shows a child owning her share of a shared courtyard problem and caring for a community space.

passage: In the computer lab, while the teacher helped someone at the back, Ojas nudged Sahil. On his screen was a photo he had taken at lunch: a classmate asleep on his desk, mouth open. 'Class group, yes? Everyone will laugh so hard.' Sahil, eleven, did laugh for a second. Then he pictured his own face up there. 'Delete it, yaar.' 'It's a joke.' 'He didn't say yes to the joke.' Ojas rolled his eyes, then sighed and dragged the photo to the bin. 'Empty the bin too,' Sahil said. Ojas did. 'Now let's finish the chart before Sir checks,' Sahil said, pulling the keyboard closer, his hands still a little shaky.

qa.q: What was in the photo Ojas wanted to share?
qa.a: A classmate asleep on his desk with his mouth open.

qa.q: What does Sahil picturing his own face suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He imagined how it would feel to be the one laughed at, which turned his laugh into concern.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Sahil did?
qa.a: A teacher could talk with the class about asking before sharing anyone's photo, and quietly thank students who stop a post like this.

qa.q: What would change for the sleeping classmate if the photo had been posted?
qa.a: He might have been teased in front of the whole class without ever agreeing to it.

grounding: Illustrates respectful digital behaviour, a child stopping a friend from sharing a classmate's photo without consent.
